about: Light inside a world's shadow (VP-L3): starlight bent through the limb of its air, reddened along the grazing path and spread out by the bending.

checks.says: number density must be zero or more, got {}
scale height must be above zero, got {}
radius must be above zero, got {}

references: Link, F. 1969, Eclipse Phenomena in Astronomy, Springer: the light in a planet's shadow is sunlight bent through its limb, reddened along the grazing path; the column along a grazing ray in an exponential atmosphere is n √(2π r H). doi:10.1007/978-3-642-86775-6

equation.name: How much air a ray grazing the limb goes through
equation.formula: N = n * sqrt(2 * pi * r * H)

n.name: molecules per cubic metre at the ray's lowest point

H.name: height over which the air thins by e

r.name: distance from the centre to the ray's lowest point

N.name: molecules per square metre along the whole grazing ray

source.text: Link, F. 1969, Eclipse Phenomena in Astronomy

explain.curious: Light skimming the edge of a world's air crosses far more of it than light coming straight down: about forty times more on Earth. That long path is why sunsets, and eclipses, are red.
explain.science: Column along a chord of an isothermal exponential atmosphere through its tangent point, to first order in H/r.

checks.says: refractivity must be zero or more, got {}
scale height must be above zero, got {}

references: Baum, W. A. and Code, A. D. 1953, A photometric observation of the occultation of sigma Arietis by Jupiter, AJ 58, 108: in an exponential atmosphere of scale height H a ray grazing at radius r is bent by θ = ν √(2πr/H), ν the refractivity at its lowest point, and the light behind is spread out by the factor 1 / (1 + D θ/H) at distance D. doi:10.1086/106829

equation.name: How far a world's air bends light skimming its limb
equation.formula: theta = nu * sqrt(2 * pi * r / H)

nu.name: n − 1 of the air at the ray's lowest point

H.name: height over which the air thins by e

r.name: distance from the centre to the ray's lowest point

theta.name: total angle the ray is turned through, radians

source.text: Baum, W. A. and Code, A. D. 1953, AJ 58, 108

explain.curious: Air bends light that skims a world's edge, a little over a degree for Earth. That is enough to throw sunset-red light into Earth's shadow and light up an eclipsed Moon.
explain.science: Refraction angle for a ray through an isothermal exponential atmosphere, ν √(2πr/H) to first order.

equation.name: How thinly the bent light is spread out behind the world

theta.name: angle the ray is turned through, radians

H.name: height over which the air thins by e

phi.name: share of the light's brightness left after the bending spreads it out

source.text: Baum, W. A. and Code, A. D. 1953, AJ 58, 108

explain.curious: Deeper air bends light more, so neighbouring rays fan apart and the bent light is spread thin. That is why an eclipsed Moon is dim as well as red.
explain.science: Refractive defocusing: rays from heights h and h + dh separate by D dθ, so the flux falls by 1/(1 + D θ/H).
